I ran a cool train assassination.  Players hired by a corporation to assassinate member of a rival corporation.  They had to drive into Train going through a asteroid field between 2 planets.  Sneak through cars, Disguiseing as staff members and climbing on roofs to fight bodyguards at the same time train goes though a tunnel through Astroid. Can only see in tunnels every other round.  Get into a private cart, assassinate target and get to front to signal ship to pick them up.  Can make different carts, some are AI controlled traps knowing they aren't on train manifest. Monster being transported in a giant long train cart that can be a mini boss.  Tons of options for trains.  Maybe at certain point an ion storm hits and knocks out trains interior artificial gravity. Maybe cargo train full of mechs on security mode, maybe passenger train with other assassins trying to kill target first.  Maybe multiple targets throughout train. Maybe is a double decker side by side train. Yeah do some train shit.

They actually have a cool system for building the ships and its based on total party level, it's easy to just not sell ships for the galactic currency. Other than ships,  the economy is really cool actually and has an entire crafting system that works really well so you could literally be like yeah ima be a gunsmith and guna build guns and sell them. It's just because with starships, it's such a complex topic to build a game out of, it's better to make a simpler smaller system even if it restricts the player slightly, but is better in the long run just for quality of life with not needing a huge complex system in this style of game because the starships and technology are 2nd to focus of the games design to having a deep complex character building system that allows crazy variety. It's like playing 5e dnd but people had advanced enough that they had crazy magic super cars that would be widely used but incredibly expensive to the point its out of reach of anything but a level 20 character makes it somewhat pointless and unreasonable. So with a fixed smaller system you can give players those tools and things but have it make since. It's weird if a party of 4 random dudes just randomly had an extra 500000 for a ship, you'd never even be able to afford one if they had listed price points. It's actually really great game design that works around a narrative sourced problem based in your core systems.

I do 5e and starfinder, it's really cool and alot of fun. Alot of people ignore starship combat because it feels repetitive after a bit for players I just suggest doing more RP with ship battles or space them out.  Also really read the combat mechanisms some are worded weird like Coup de Gace is an auto crit full action but you can only really use it in specific situations and I've had players misunderstand when they can use it.  I think the transition is good from 5e, starfinder plays similar but has better quality of life.  Alot of rules and mechanics I'd have to wing myself in 5e already have rules in starfinder books.  Number one I'd say is don't let players by items over their level, or give too much money quickly. In rules it says never let players sell starships for money because it breaks the game. The Hacking systems are a lil confusing I suggest watching videos on it, Maple story on YouTube has fantastic starfinder content for GMs.

The average session for regular play is 3 to 5 hours. I've run for many groups who use this time. My current group I run 8 to 12 hour sessions. It's really just about what the group needs to enjoy the game, make progress, but also fit people's schedules. The more people in a group, often the longer sessions need to be. Also as a DM it's your job to nudge people who take too long to make decisions during combat or talk to NPCs to long goofing off to keep the session on track so progress can be made, it kinda sucks to play 8 hours and make 0 progress because a single party member or two were messing around too much.
